Index.title: THE ELITE
Index.hero_subtitle: Explore the biographies of the nation's finest through a unique interactive visual experience.
Index.why_description: In an era of accelerating events, we return to seek steadfastness from a generation that shaped history with their sincerity. 'Nokhbet El Sahaba' is not merely a website, but a visual journey sailing through the lives of the Ten Promised Paradise, witnessing the pivotal moments that changed the face of the world.
Index.intro_quote: They were the ones who bridged the Earth and the Heavens. Men who did not just make history, they were history itself. Ten moons that illuminated the nation's path—each with a story to be told, and a legacy that never fades.
Index.intro_footer: Prepare yourself... for we stand now in the presence of the Immortals.

abu_bakr.nickname: The One Manumitted from the Fire
abu_bakr.bio: If the faith of Abu Bakr were weighed against the faith of the people of the earth, it would outweigh them. The first man to embrace Islam, the companion of the Hijra, and the pillar who kept the nation firm upon the Prophet's ﷺ passing.

omar.bio: Had there been a prophet after me, it would have been Omar. He through whom Allah empowered Islam and distinguished truth from falsehood. The giant of Islam whose justice echoed across the earth.

othman.bio: Should I not feel shy before a man whom even the angels are shy of? Renowned for his deep modesty and immense generosity, he compiled the Quran and illuminated his heart with the light of faith.

ali.bio: Are you not content to be to me as Aaron was to Moses? The gateway to the city of knowledge, the hero of Khaybar, and the first youth to embrace Islam. He combined valor in the field with eloquence of the tongue.

talha.bio: Whoever wishes to look at a martyr walking upon the earth, let him look at Talha. One of the foremost in Islam, the knight who shielded the Prophet ﷺ with his own body at Uhud until his hand was paralyzed.

zubair.bio: Every prophet has a disciple, and my disciple is Al-Zubair. The cousin of the Prophet ﷺ and the first to unsheathe a sword for the sake of Allah. A knight who fought with the strength of an entire army.

abdurrahman.bio: May Allah bless what you have given. One of the six members of the Shura council, and the merchant who dedicated his entire wealth to Islam. He remained an ascetic despite his vast riches.

saad.nickname: The Maternal Uncle of the Messenger
saad.bio: Shoot, O Saad! May my father and mother be sacrificed for you. The first to fire an arrow in the way of Allah and the hero of Qadisiyyah who extinguished the fires of the Persians forever.

saeed.bio: One of the foremost in Islam and the knight of Yarmouk. A man of deep asceticism and piety, he was one of the ten to whom the Prophet ﷺ bore witness of Paradise while they still walked the earth.

abu_ubaida.bio: Every nation has a trustee, and the trustee of this nation is Abu Ubaida. The conqueror of the Levant and the ascetic leader who prioritized the afterlife over all worldly gains.

Index.footerout: Those Are the Ones Whom Allah Has Guided
Index.footerp: These are not just names in the pages of history, but beacons that illuminated the path of truth and justice for humanity. Their lives are an endless source of inspiration, and their stories are nourishment for the soul. We invite you to dive into the details of their lives, to draw from their courage, wisdom, and generosity what can light your own path.

hero.subtitle: The First Man to Believe
hero.title: Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq
hero.verse: The second of two, when they were both in the cave

timeline.label: A Journey of Truth and Devotion

card1.title: Lineage & Birth
card1.body: Abdullah ibn Abi Quhafa was born in Mecca two years and six months after the Year of the Elephant. He was raised in one of the most distinguished households of Quraysh, the clan of Banu Taym. His father Abu Quhafa and his mother Umm al-Khayr were both people of standing. He grew up embodying the noblest of character even in the age of ignorance — he never once drank wine, and never once prostrated before an idol, for his pure nature knew instinctively that these idols could neither benefit nor harm.

card2.title: His Standing Among Quraysh
card2.body: Al-Siddiq was a prosperous and successful cloth merchant, widely known for his honesty and trustworthiness. People sought his counsel for his sound judgment and encyclopedic knowledge of Arab lineages. Quraysh would consult him in matters of blood money and tribal obligations, and whatever he undertook, they trusted him in it. His friendship with the Prophet ﷺ predated the revelation itself, born of a profound resemblance in character — he was the companion before the message.

traits.label: Appearance:
traits.body: He was slender in build, fair in complexion, with light hair on his cheeks. He carried an air of dignity and gravity, softened by a tenderness of heart and a deep compassion.

titles.label: His Titles:
titles.body: He was called Al-Atiq for the beauty of his face, and some say because God freed him from the Fire. He was called Al-Siddiq for being the first to believe the Prophet ﷺ without a moment's hesitation.

list.title: Siyar A'lam al-Nubala
list.author: Imam al-Dhahabi (biography of Al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him)

faith.sectionSubtitle: I called no one to Islam but he hesitated… except Abu Bakr

card1.title: Belief Without Hesitation
card1.body: Abu Bakr's conversion was no passing event — it was the fruit of years of deep friendship with the Prophet ﷺ. When the revelation descended, the Prophet ﷺ went to him and presented the matter. Without asking for a sign or demanding a miracle, he believed on the spot. The Prophet ﷺ said of him: 'I called no one to Islam but he paused and deliberated — except Abu Bakr. When I told him, he did not waver nor hesitate for a moment.'

card2.title: The Man Who Brought a Nation
card2.body: Al-Siddiq did not stop at his own faith. He immediately set out to call those he trusted. Through him, Islam reached giants who would later shake the earth — five of the ten promised Paradise: Uthman ibn Affan, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Saad ibn Abi Waqqas, and Talha ibn Ubaydullah. Each of them stands in the scale of his good deeds, for he was the key that opened their hearts to the light.

card3.title: Spending Without Fear of Poverty
card3.body: In Mecca, the weak were being tortured for their faith. Al-Siddiq deployed his mightiest weapon: his wealth. He purchased and freed seven souls who were being tormented for the sake of God, foremost among them Bilal ibn Rabah, the caller to prayer of the Messenger ﷺ. His father Abu Quhafa said to him: 'My son, I see you freeing the weak and frail — why not free strong men who could protect you?' Al-Siddiq replied with certainty: 'Father, I only seek what is with God.'
card3.quote: Father, I only seek what is with God.

list.title: Al-Sira al-Nabawiyya
list.author: Ibn Hisham (account of Abu Bakr's conversion)

loyalty.sectionSubtitle: A Love Story That Came Before the Journey
loyalty.body: Al-Siddiq's selection for the migration was no accident — it was a decision made by the heart before the revelation gave its leave. When the Prophet ﷺ asked: 'Companionship, O Abu Bakr?', Al-Siddiq burst into tears of overwhelming joy. He did not weep from fear of the death that lay in wait for them both — he wept because he had been chosen to be the shadow of God's Messenger ﷺ.
loyalty.reflection: If I am killed, I am but one man. But if he ﷺ is killed, the entire nation is lost.
loyalty.closingPoem: Is it not from love that Al-Siddiq wept? Yes — and from sacrifice that minds were left in awe.

cave.sectionTag: The Moment That Held History's Breath
cave.sectionTitleHighlight: When They Were Both in the Cave
cave.imageAlt: The second of two in the cave
cave.body1: In the darkness of the Cave of Thawr, Al-Siddiq had no fear for his own life — his heart trembled with terror for the light of prophethood. When the feet of the idolaters drew so close he could see them through the cracks in the rock, he whispered through tears of devotion: 'O Messenger of God, if any of them looked down at his feet, he would see us.'
cave.whisper: O Messenger of God, if any of them looked down at his feet, he would see us.
cave.body2: In that moment, Al-Siddiq was not thinking of his trade or his family — he was thinking only of how to shield the body of the Prophet ﷺ with his own chest. Then came the voice of tranquility that shook the mountains of Mecca:
cave.divineResponse: Do not grieve; indeed God is with us.
cave.body3: Fear turned to serenity, and constriction became a way out — so that the world might know that when God is with you, there is no room for the impossible.

medina.sectionSubtitle: The Beginning of a New Era
medina.imageAlt: Arrival at the City of the Prophet
medina.body1: The blessed caravan arrived at Quba, and it was a day the likes of which Medina had never witnessed. Al-Siddiq stood shielding the Prophet ﷺ from the scorching sun with his cloak, as the people rushed forward in eager wonder — unsure which of the two was the Messenger, until they saw the shadow of Al-Siddiq and understood the rank of the companion beside the one he accompanied.
medina.body2: Medina was no mere stopover — it was a home that Al-Siddiq built with his wealth and effort. He purchased the land for the mosque, and together with the Prophet ﷺ laid the foundations of the new state. He remained the inseparable shadow, the counselor whom no one could surpass in opinion or advice.

foundation.imageAlt: The building of the Prophet's Mosque
foundation.body1: The stability of Medina could not have been achieved without the blessed wealth of Al-Siddiq. When the Prophet ﷺ wished to build his mosque, Abu Bakr purchased the land from two orphans — making him the first financier of the greatest edifice in the history of Islam.
foundation.quote: Al-Siddiq in Medina was like the Prophet's own shadow that never left him — his hand with which he built, his mind he consulted in every matter. No one preceded him in digging a well, feeding the hungry, or reconciling hearts.
foundation.body2: In every corner of Medina, Abu Bakr left his mark — from organizing the market to managing the affairs of the Muslims. He was the faithful minister who bore the weight of the nascent state upon his shoulders with love and the deepest humility.
achievements: Purchased the land of the mosque

steadfastness.body: Medina shook. Men wept. Minds reeled. Then Al-Siddiq emerged. With a heart filled with certainty, he spoke his immortal words:
steadfastness.immortalWords: Whoever worshipped Muhammad — Muhammad has died. Whoever worshipped God — God is Ever-Living and shall never die.
steadfastness.aftermath: In that moment, he was the pillar that kept the nation from shattering, and restored it to the path of truth with the steadfastness of prophets.

caliphate.imageAlt: The caliphate of Al-Siddiq and the Ridda Wars
caliphate.body1: He took up the burden of the caliphate and proved to be the decisive leader whose resolve never bent. He dispatched the army of Usama ibn Zayd despite every pressure to withdraw, waged the Ridda Wars with the heart of a lion, and reunited the Muslims at a time when everyone thought their state had come to an end. He sought neither prestige nor power — he was simply fulfilling his covenant with his beloved ﷺ.
caliphate.body2: Yet even in the midst of war, he did not forget the compilation of the Holy Quran. Fearing its loss with the martyrdom of its memorizers, he ordered it gathered into a single manuscript — an act that became the light illuminating the path of the nation for all the centuries that followed. The caliphate of Al-Siddiq was an epic of building and unification, cementing the foundations of the state and preserving the community of believers.

highlights2.quranCompilation: the compilation of the Holy Quran

farewell.sectionSubtitle: In the Company of the Beloved ﷺ
farewell.body: On a quiet night in Medina, the soul of Al-Siddiq returned to its Creator. He was buried beside his beloved ﷺ — the second of two in the cave, and the second of two in the grave. He left behind a united nation, a steadfast state, and a fragrant legacy that fills the world with light and guidance. He was the finest successor to the finest of predecessors. May God have mercy on him with a vast mercy, and reward him on behalf of Islam and the Muslims with the greatest of rewards.

highlights.dualCompanion: the second of two in the cave, and the second of two in the grave

farewell.closingTag: The Elite of the Companions — Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq

uthmanBinAffan.title: Uthman ibn Affan
uthmanBinAffan.subtitle: Dhul-Nurayn (The One with Two Lights)
uthmanBinAffan.description: The third of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, one of the Ten Companions promised Paradise, the man whom the angels of the Most Merciful were shy of.

lineageSection.title: Lineage and Kunya
lineageSection.fullLineage: Uthman ibn Affan ibn Abi al-As ibn Umayya al-Qurashi
lineageSection.lineageDetail: His lineage meets that of the Prophet ﷺ at the fourth grandfather (Abd Manaf). He was from Banu Umayya, one of the most noble tribes of Quraysh.
lineageSection.nicknameDetail: He was known by the kunyah (Abu Abdullah) and (Abu Layla). His most famous title was (Dhul-Nurayn — Bearer of Two Lights) because he married Ruqayyah and then Umm Kulthum, the two daughters of the Prophet ﷺ.
lineageSection.birthDetail: He was born in Makkah al-Mukarramah approximately six years after the Year of the Elephant.

islamAndMarriage.title: His Islam and Marriage
islamAndMarriage.step1_desc: Uthman — may Allah be pleased with him — embraced Islam early at the very beginning of the call, when Abu Bakr al-Siddiq invited him to it. He was among the earliest forerunners through whom Allah honored the religion.
islamAndMarriage.step2_title: Marriage to Ruqayyah (peace be upon her)
islamAndMarriage.step2_desc: The Prophet ﷺ gave him his daughter Ruqayyah in marriage. She emigrated with him to Abyssinia and then to Madinah. They were known as 'the most beautiful couple any human eye had ever seen.'
islamAndMarriage.step3_desc: Ruqayyah passed away on the day of the victory of Badr. Uthman grieved deeply, saddened by the severing of his bond with the Prophet ﷺ, but the Messenger comforted him with glad tidings.
islamAndMarriage.step4_title: Marriage to Umm Kulthum and the Title Dhul-Nurayn
islamAndMarriage.step4_desc: The Prophet ﷺ then gave him his second daughter Umm Kulthum in marriage. After her passing, the Prophet said: 'Had we a third, we would have given her to you in marriage, O Uthman.' Thus he was given the title (Dhul-Nurayn — Bearer of Two Lights).

paradiseSection.title: His Station of Virtue and Glad Tidings of Divine Pleasure
paradiseSection.card1_desc: One of the early Muslims whom the Prophet ﷺ bore witness to their entry into Paradise in a single gathering.
paradiseSection.card2_desc: When the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Should I not be shy of a man whom the angels are shy of?' — due to the greatness of his purity.
paradiseSection.card3_desc: The Messenger ﷺ gave him the glad tidings: 'Every prophet has a companion, and my companion in Paradise is Uthman.'
paradiseSection.card4_desc: The Prophet ﷺ promised him Paradise through a trial that would befall him, and he remained patient until he met his Lord as a martyr.
paradiseSection.card5_desc: Allah honored him with the preservation of the Quran; he united the Ummah upon the 'Mushaf al-Imam' (the Imam's Codex).
paradiseSection.card6_desc: About him the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Nothing Uthman does after today will harm him' — after he outfitted the army.
paradiseSection.card7_desc: He emigrated with his family to Abyssinia and then to Madinah, earning the full reward of the patient emigrants.
paradiseSection.card8_desc: He was distinguished by a honor granted to no other human being — marriage to two daughters of a Prophet ﷺ.
paradiseSection.card9_title: The One Who Quenched the Muslims
paradiseSection.card9_desc: He purchased the Well of Rumah from his own wealth and made it a perpetual endowment (waqf) for all Muslims.

tajerAlRahman.label: Giving and Generosity
tajerAlRahman.title: The Merchant of the Most Merciful: Spending in the Path of Allah
tajerAlRahman.description: Uthman — may Allah be pleased with him — was not merely a wealthy merchant; he was an outstanding model of harnessing wealth in service of faith and humanity. His compassion and generosity shone brightest in the darkest of circumstances — from purchasing the Well of Rumah with his own money to quench the thirst of Muslims, to equipping the Army of Hardship for the Battle of Tabuk, to expanding the Prophet's Mosque.
tajerAlRahman.callout: Nothing Uthman does after today will harm him

subtasks.army: Equipping the Army of Hardship (Battle of Tabuk)
subtasks.well: The Well of Rumah and its story of quenching the Muslims

quranCollection.label: The Greatest Achievement
quranCollection.title: The Compilation of the Quran and Unification of the Mushaf
quranCollection.description: As the Islamic state expanded and tongues became mixed through the conquests of new lands, Uthman ibn Affan — may Allah be pleased with him — sensed an imminent danger threatening the unity of the Ummah: disagreement in the recitation of the Book of Allah. By a wise and sovereign decision, with the consensus of the senior Companions, he ordered the Quran to be written in the dialect of Quraysh in which the revelation had descended, to serve as a single authoritative reference beyond any doubt. He gifted the world the 'Mushaf al-Imami' which protected the Wise Reminder from distortion and fragmentation across the centuries — making this achievement the greatest bond that preserved Muslim unity and united their hearts upon a common word until the Day of Judgment.
quranCollection.distributionLabel: The regions to which the Mushaf was sent:
quranCollection.regions: Makkah al-Mukarramah, Al-Sham, Kufa, Basra, Yemen, Bahrain, and Madinah al-Munawwarah
quranCollection.callout: The Mushaf al-Imami: Unity of the Word
quranCollection.figcaption: The Mushaf of Uthman ibn Affan — may Allah be pleased with him

uthmanBinAffan.sec-title: Achievements of the Era of Uthman ibn Affan
uthmanBinAffan.sec-dec: The caliphate of Dhul-Nurayn was not merely a continuation of what came before — it was a golden age that witnessed the first naval fleet in Islamic history, the greatest wave of conquests spanning three continents, and a solid administrative organization that preserved the prestige and stability of the state.

wars.secc-des: An era of expansion, conquests, generosity, and prosperity

list.name: Conquests of the East and Persia

content.introduction: Completing the march begun by al-Faruq Umar to end the Sassanid presence and spread Islam across the regions of Central Asia.
content.causes: Some Persian factions broke their treaties after the death of Umar ibn al-Khattab, necessitating the securing of the state's eastern borders.
content.events: Armies marched toward the eastern regions, subduing cities that had revolted and opening new territories the Muslims had never reached before.
content.results: The complete collapse of the Sassanid Empire, vast new lands entering Islam, and the flow of spoils into the treasury.

list.name: Conquests of Armenia and the Caucasus

content.introduction: Expansion into the mountainous northern regions to secure the borders of Al-Sham and Iraq from Byzantine and Khazar raids.
content.causes: The Byzantines used the mountainous regions to launch attacks against Muslims, and Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan requested that this front be secured.
content.events: The campaigns culminated in the conquest of Armenia and Azerbaijan, with armies reaching the rugged peaks of the Caucasus.
content.results: Muslim control over northern trade routes and fortification of the state against Byzantine attacks from the north.

content.introduction: Setting out westward from Egypt to conquer the regions of Ifriqiyyah (present-day Tunisia) and spread Islam across the greater Maghreb.
content.causes: Securing Egypt's western borders and cutting off Byzantine hopes of regaining control over North Africa.
content.events: The great Battle of Sbeitla took place, in which the Muslims triumphed over King Gregory (Gregorius), who had dominated the region.
content.results: The fall of Byzantine influence in Tunisia, payment of tribute to the Muslims, and the paving of the way for the future conquest of the Maghreb and Andalusia.
leaders: Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi al-Sarh

content.introduction: The first naval campaign in Islamic history, targeting the island of Cyprus to establish a defensive base in the Mediterranean Sea.
content.causes: The Byzantines used the island of Cyprus as a supply hub for their fleets and a base to attack the coasts of Al-Sham and Egypt.
content.events: Uthman ordered the construction of the first Islamic fleet, and the ships sailed from the coasts of Al-Sham, opening the island through a peace treaty.
content.results: The establishment of the first Islamic naval force, the securing of Muslim coastlines, and the imposition of tribute on the people of Cyprus.

content.introduction: Strengthening defenses and fortifications in Al-Sham to face continuous Byzantine threats.
content.causes: Repeated Byzantine Empire attempts to recapture Antioch and northern Al-Sham.
content.events: Building fortresses, restoring border strongholds, and conducting summer and winter campaigns to pursue the remnants of Byzantine forces.
content.results: Stabilization of security in Al-Sham and prevention of any Byzantine penetration into the Muslim heartland.

content.introduction: Re-opening Alexandria and consolidating Islamic rule in Egypt after a Byzantine-backed rebellion attempt.
content.causes: A Byzantine fleet landed in Alexandria with support from some of its inhabitants in an attempt to break the peace treaty.
content.events: A fierce battle was fought in which the Muslims recaptured the city and expelled the Byzantine forces from it entirely.
content.results: Affirming Islamic sovereignty over Egypt and transforming Alexandria into a major naval base.

content.introduction: The conquest of the historical region of Kerman in the Persian lands.
content.causes: Completing the conquest of the remaining provinces belonging to the former Sassanid Empire.
content.events: Clashes with local forces ended with the opening of the city and the spread of Islam within it.
content.results: Securing the route toward Sind and India and increasing the state's resources.

content.introduction: The conquest of the vast region of Khorasan, the gateway to Central Asia.
content.causes: The presence of remnants of the Persian army there, and the geostrategic importance of the region.
content.events: The main cities — such as Merv, Nishapur, and Herat — were opened after sieges and multiple battles.
content.results: Khorasan transformed into a major Islamic cultural and military center in the East.

content.introduction: The conquest of the Sistan region, located in the border area between present-day Iran and Afghanistan.
content.causes: Securing the state's eastern frontiers and preventing infiltration from the mountainous regions.
content.events: The Islamic armies advanced through deserts and mountains and opened 'Zaranj,' the capital of the region.
content.results: The spread of Islam in distant provinces and the expansion of the Caliphate's influence to encompass present-day Afghan territories.

content.description: Uthman — may Allah be pleased with him — adhered to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ, followed the path of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, relied on consultation (shura), and did not intervene in people's affairs except when necessary.
content.impact: This led to societal stability in the first half of his caliphate and the spread of a spirit of disciplined freedom within the bounds of Islamic law.
examples: His commitment to the decisions of the shura council in appointing governors
Application of the prescribed legal punishments without exception

content.description: He consolidated the Shura Council comprising senior Companions to participate in running the state and making decisions.
content.impact: Strengthening the unity among senior Companions and ensuring the soundness of momentous decisions related to conquests and governance.

content.description: Uthman — may Allah be pleased with him — was among the first to organize the judiciary and establish courts in the Islamic state as independent institutions.
content.impact: Separating the judiciary from the mosque in some regions to increase the court's prestige and organize court records.

achievements.name: Administration and Organization of the Provinces

content.description: He reorganized the provinces and appointed new governors in the best interest of the state, relying on consultation with those of sound judgment.
changes: Meticulous monitoring of governors' conduct and holding them accountable
Development of financial bureaus (diwans) in the newly opened regions
content.impact: Achieving administrative balance across a vast state and ensuring rights reached their rightful owners.

content.description: He merged some smaller provinces together to achieve better administrative and military efficiency.
examples: Unifying the provinces of Al-Sham under a single command (Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan)
Annexing Bahrain to the province of Basra
content.impact: Facilitating military decision-making and consolidating the financial and administrative resources of each region.

fitna_and_martyrdom.title: The Fitna and Martyrdom (Patience and Steadfastness)

events.name: Events of the Siege and His Stance on Protecting Bloodshed

content.description: Uthman was besieged in his home for forty days, during which water and food were withheld from him. Despite the ability of senior Companions and their sons — such as al-Hasan and al-Husayn — to fight the besiegers, the Caliph firmly refused to allow a single drop of Muslim blood to be shed for his sake.
content.heroic_stance: His famous words: 'I adjure every person who owes me a right to hold back his hand' — choosing martyrdom over causing chaos in the city of the Messenger of Allah.
content.impact: Uthman entrenched the principle of patient steadfastness and set the most magnificent example of selflessness and protection of the Ummah's unity in its most difficult moments.

events.name: The Story of His Martyrdom While Reading the Quran

content.description: On the morning of a Friday, while the Caliph was fasting and reciting the verses of the Book of Allah, the rebels stormed his home and attacked him as he sat between his hands holding his Mushaf.
content.final_moments: His pure blood flowed onto the very Mushaf he had compiled — specifically upon the words of Allah: (And Allah will be sufficient for you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing).
content.legacy: He ascended as a patient and hopeful martyr, bringing to a close the longest caliphate of the Rightly Guided era and opening a new chapter in the history of the Ummah.

quotes_section.title: Sayings and Wisdom
quotes_section.subtitle: From His Sermons on Asceticism and Piety

quotes.text: O people, fear Allah the Exalted, for taqwa (God-consciousness) is a blessing. The wisest of people is he who takes himself to account and works for what comes after death, and seeks from the light of Allah a light for the darkness of the grave. Let every servant fear that Allah will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection when he had been sighted. Know that whoever has Allah with him fears nothing, and whoever has Allah against him — whom can he hope in after that?

Indeed, Allah has given you this world so that you may seek the Hereafter through it — so do not lean upon it, for this world will come to an end and the final destination is to Allah the Exalted. Therefore, fear Allah, for His taqwa is a shield from His wrath and a protection from His punishment.

Every thing has a blight, and every blessing has a defect. The blight of this religion and the defect of this blessing are those who constantly find fault and slander — they show you what you love and conceal what you hate. They are a riffraff like ostriches, following the first caller. As for the envier — it suffices you that he grieves at the time of your joy.

The best of servants is he who guards himself and seeks protection in the Book of Allah the Exalted, looks at the grave and weeps, and says: 'It is the first station of the Hereafter and the last station of this world. Whoever faces hardship there — what follows will be no easier. And whoever finds ease there — what follows will be no harder.'

You are more in need of a leader who acts than a leader who merely speaks. This world is lush and enticing and many have been drawn to it — so do not lean upon it and do not trust it, for it is untrustworthy. Know that it will not leave anyone who does not leave it first.
If our hearts were truly pure, we would never tire of the words of our Lord. And truly I detest that any day should pass over me without me looking into the Mushaf.
